extracted_by: hand, T-0294 — the Democrat read, December 1834
note: Vol. II No. 1, the first number of Volume II. FOUR OF THIS ISSUE'S TWENTY-FOUR COLUMNS WERE TRANSCRIBED WITH A TESSERACT FALLBACK RATHER THAN THE VISION READING — page 3 columns 4 and 5, page 4 columns 1 and 2 — and they are by a wide margin the most legible type in the month: the fire ordinance, Peter Cohen's placement, the Democrat's own corner lot and the building-materials prices all stand whole there where the Vision columns beside them are shredded. Nine of the sixteen claims here come from those four columns. The remaining twenty columns alternate two physical columns line by line in the usual way, and where a supply below is read off the other half of a printed line the note names the lines it came from. No post-office letter list of any office stands in this issue.

claims.normalized: Town Ordinance. At a meeting of the President and Trustees of the Town of Chicago, held at “the Exchange,’ in said town, on the 3d day of November A. D. 18[3]4: — The following Ordinance was adopted, to wit: An Ordinance for the further prevention of Fires. — Whereas, it has been represented by sundry citizens, house-holders and owners of property in the town of Chicago, that great danger of destruction to their property and to that of the community at large exists, by means of a practice too generally indulged, viz: that of carrying fire from one house to another without care or caution, and whereas, the President and Trustees of the Town of Chicago, have been called upon by their fellow citizens, to adopt measures for the prevention of the said practice in future, Therefore Be it and it hereby is Ordained by the President and Trustees of the [T]own of Chicago, That hereafter it shall not be lawful for any person or persons to carry or convey fire brands or coals of fire from one house or building to anot[h]er within the limits of the corporation, unless the same be carried or conveyed in a covered earth[e]rn of fire proof vessel. Any person offending against the provisions of this ordinance shall be liable to a fine of Five Dollars for each and every offence to be recovered in complaint before any Justice of the peace in like manner as other f[i]nes are by law recoverable. This Ordinance to take effect and be in force from and after the 12th day of Nov. A. D. 1834. J[N]O. H. KINZIE, Pres’t. Bd. Trustees of the T[o]wn of Chicago. Attest — E. W. Casey, Clerk [pro tem.]

occupations: President of the Board of Trustees of the Town of Chicago
Clerk of the Board of Trustees

claims.notes: FIRE IS CARRIED FROM HOUSE TO HOUSE BY HAND IN THIS TOWN, AND THE TRUSTEES OUTLAW IT. The single most physical thing this ordinance says about the town is why it was needed: in a settlement with no matches to speak of, a household without a fire fetched live coals from a neighbour's hearth and carried them home in the open. The remedy the Trustees allow is the detail worth keeping — the coals may still be carried, but only 'in a covered earthen or fire proof vessel'. The meeting is at the Exchange, which is the third November sitting this corpus has placed there (T-0293), and it is one of at most a handful of buildings in the town that the President and Trustees use. This column is one of the four in the issue that the deposit transcribed with a Tesseract fallback rather than the Vision reading, and it is legible end to end where the interleaved columns beside it are not — the whole ordinance stands here as one unbroken run of lines, which is why it is quoted whole. The date '1234' in the dateline is a recognition-class error for 1834 and is corrected; the ordinance's own commencement clause, 12 November 1834, fixes it.

claims.notes: A CORNER, NAMED: SOUTH WATER AND CLARK. The building is the Democrat's own former office, shared with W. Kimball's store, and this is the printing that gives its corner without a supply. The November notice of the same lot (1834-11-12 c003) breaks off before the streets, and the October one (1834-10-08 c005) has the occupancy but not the corner. Two facts stand together here and both are usable: a building large enough to hold a newspaper office and a store at once, and the intersection it stands on. 'Possession given on the first of June next' dates the vacancy to June 1835, one month before the scene date — so whoever is in it on 1 July 1835 is not the Democrat and not Kimball.

claims.notes: WHAT THE TOWN PAID FOR WHAT IT WAS BUILT OF, IN THE MONTH IT WAS BUYING IT. The Chicago Prices Current runs weekly in the Democrat and 1834-11-12 c007 extracted its provisions half; this is its building-materials band, which nothing had taken yet. Poplar lumber at $20–$23 the thousand feet, shingles at $2.50–$3.00, square timber at 5–6 cents the running foot and brick at $6.00 the thousand are the four numbers the reconstruction's fabric decisions actually turn on. Note what the ratio says: brick at $6 a thousand against lumber at $20 a thousand feet is not the price signal of a brick town, and the town this corpus describes is overwhelmingly a wooden one. The stone, lime and wood rows are cut by the column edge and their figures are marked absent rather than guessed — the leading letter of each row name is also cut away by the segmenter and is supplied.

claims.notes: NINETY FEET BY FORTY-FIVE, FINISHED, IN KINZIE'S ADDITION — AND THE OWNER SAYS IT IS THE BEST FINISHED ROOM IN THE TOWN. Kinzie's Addition is the North Division, north of the main river, and a single floor of 4,050 square feet there in 1834 is a large building by the standards of everything else in this corpus: Temple's three-storey store house on the river is 40 by 60. The claim it makes for itself — 'by far the best finished rooms' — is the advertiser's, not the paper's, and is recorded as his boast rather than as fact. John H. Kinzie is the same man who signs the fire ordinance as President of the Board of Trustees (c001). The word after 'in the' is cut away by the column edge; 'town' is a supply and is bracketed, and the compass word before 'part of Chicago' is gone entirely and is left as an absence.

'Having erected an addition to his Store House, he is now enabled to receive a considerable quantity of merchandize in store' is a documented enlargement of a documented building, dated no later than the advertisement's 4 June dateline — not a new structure but a bigger one, which is a different thing to model. Carver is already in this corpus as the lumber yard where an important auction was held (1834-11-05 c011) and as one half of David Carver & Co, so his premises carry a yard as well as a store house. The weekly Saturday auction is the other fact worth keeping: a fixed, recurring gathering at a fixed place on South Water Street. This is page 4 column 1, one of the issue's Tesseract-fallback columns; the right-hand half of every printed line is cut away into column 2 and the supplies here are read off it, at lines 3869-3956. The surname is cut away at line 3801 and is supplied from this same issue: page 3 column 2 line 3054 prints 'DAVID CARVI, & CO' over a flour advertisement, and David Carver is already the corpus's storage, commission and lumber merchant on this street.

claims.notes: HOGUE & CO ARE NEXT DOOR TO P. PRUYNE & CO. The stock has been claimed for November (1834-11-05 c002) with the address line cut away. Here the anchor survives, split across the segmenter's two halves of the same printed line — 'next door to to ruyne' on line 3198 and 'cos' on line 3201, with the firm's own name printed between them — and the following week's issue confirms it: chicago_democrat_1834_12_10 page 3 column 3 line 2932 reads 'next door lo P. Pr' and column 4 line 3175 reads 'yue and co's.', which is the same sentence cut in the same place. Peter Pruyne is the town's druggist and a documented advertiser, so this is one documented storefront against another. The street is not stated in either printing and is left absent rather than inferred.

claims.notes: THE NOVEMBER READING OF THIS ADVERTISEMENT NAMED THE WRONG WOMAN AND THE WRONG TOWN, AND THIS PRINTING SAYS SO. Claim c002 of chicago_democrat_1834_11_26 read the milliner as '[Mrs.] HERMAN, formerly of White [Plains?] N. Y.' off a shredded column, marking the town with a query because White Pigeon was the likelier name. Both readings were wrong. A week later the same advertisement is set legibly enough to give 'MRS. H. SHERMAN' and 'White Creek' — the Herman is a lost initial and a dropped S, and White Creek is a real town in Washington County, New York. That is a correction to a claim already in this corpus, not a new business, and it is recorded here rather than by editing the November file: both mentions stand with their dates, as the corpus README requires. The placement moves too. November read the shop as somewhere against the Mansion House with the preposition cut away; here it is 'a room in the house occupied by […] hall, two doors […] of the Mansion House' — so she is a lodger in someone else's building, two doors from the Mansion House, and the compass word is still cut away and is still not supplied. The occupant's name survives only as 'hall' and could be a surname or the tail of a word; it is not resolved.
